subject: Cognitive Science
title: Classical Conditioning
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Classical Conditioning.

hook.text: Pavlov rang a bell before feeding his dogs. Soon the bell alone made them drool. Learning by association.

buildup.text: Classical conditioning pairs a neutral signal with a meaningful one until the signal triggers a response.

discovery.text: The bell became a conditioned stimulus. Salivation to the bell became a conditioned response.

twist.text: It works on humans too. A phone buzz triggers a dopamine spike before you even see the message.

climax.text: Advertisers exploit it constantly: pair a product with pleasure and the product itself feels good.

punchline.text: Your brain links signals to meaning automatically.

quiz.question: What is a conditioned stimulus?
options: A previously neutral signal that triggers a learned response

details.summary: Pavlov discovered that pairing a neutral stimulus with a meaningful one creates a learned association. After repeated pairings of a bell with food, dogs salivated at the bell alone. Classical conditioning explains phobias, advertising effects, and many automatic emotional responses in everyday life.
details.whyItMatters: Classical conditioning is one of the most fundamental learning mechanisms. It operates below conscious awareness and shapes emotional responses, preferences, and habits throughout life.
takeaways: Neutral stimuli become meaningful through repeated pairing
The response transfers from the unconditioned to conditioned stimulus
Extinction occurs when the association is no longer reinforced

faq.question: How does classical conditioning create phobias?
faq.answer: A neutral stimulus paired with a frightening experience becomes a conditioned fear trigger. A child bitten by a dog may develop a dog phobia because dogs became associated with pain and fear. The emotional response generalizes to all dogs, not just the one that bit.

faq.question: Can classical conditioning be reversed?
faq.answer: Yes, through extinction. Repeated exposure to the conditioned stimulus without the unconditioned stimulus gradually weakens the association. Exposure therapy for phobias works on this principle.
